children: BlackRock will offer American workers a chance to invest more like a multibillion-dollar pension.

The world's largest investment firm by assets under management said it would work with corporate clients to build customizable funds for 401(k) plans that can include slices of public stocks and bonds, private assets and even annuities that provide guaranteed income in retirement.

The new framework aims to resemble the menu of options offered to public-employee pension plans, university endowments and other deep-pocketed institutions that hire firms like BlackRock to manage their money.

Most corporate 401(k) plans tend to default employees into target-date funds, or those that invest in a mix of stocks and bonds that shifts as the employee gets closer to her or his "target date," or retirement age.
BlackRock said it would work with corporate clients to analyze the demographics and wages of their workforces, among other factors, to help inform investment choices.

For example, a manufacturing company with a union workforce that has an early average retirement age and an existing defined-benefit pension might have different needs for its 401(k) plan than a tech company that offers no pension benefits and pays employees with corporate stock, said Nick Nefouse, BlackRock's global head of retirement solutions.

BlackRock wants to address those differences and says it can now use technology to bring customized features to companies and plans of all sizes. That is especially important as companies consider new options that BlackRock and other investment managers are rolling out, including target-date funds that incorporate defined retirement income and private assets.

"We're trying to take the best of what 401(k)s have done, such as portability and ownership by the individual, and combine that with the best of what pensions did, which is professional management, long-term thinking and certainty through income in retirement," Nefouse said in an interview.

A firm later acquired by BlackRock had helped pioneer target-date funds in the 1990s. The funds now take in a majority of the money flowing into 401(k) plans in the U.S., according to Vanguard data. They have been lauded for helping assure savers' investments match their risk tolerance and proximity to retirement.
Firms such as BlackRock are now looking for ways to improve these funds once investors reach that target date.
"The problem is that we designed this whole system just to maximize savings, maximize account value, and then you get to retirement, we hand the money back to you and say 'good luck,'" Nefouse said.

BlackRock, Vanguard, Fidelity Investments and State Street have all recently announced new funds that give investors the option of buying an annuity before or after their retirement date that guarantees some level of income for the rest of their lives.

The latest debate in retirement investing centers on private assets. President Trump signed an executive order in 2025 directing federal agencies and regulators to clear the path for assets such as private equity, private credit and real estate into 401(k) plans.

Private-asset funds have long been a major component of pension-fund and insurance-company portfolios. Proponents of private-market funds in 401(k)s argue that they can be less correlated to public stocks and offer premium returns in exchange for less liquidity. Skeptics point to higher management fees and less transparency from managers.
The decision whether to offer private assets in a corporate 401(k) plan ultimately comes down to the company offering it and its goals.

"If private markets can help you reach or beat that objective, net of all fees, then we think that's a good tool," Nefouse added. "What we're not doing is saying we've got target-date funds, we've got private markets, and we should just push that together for everyone."
